# Umbraco Rules

Project conventions, enforced by code in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco` where possible. The short version of the ten UmbraCommandments.

1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. Compositions are for meta, settings, CTAs. Litmus test: *if we remove this composition later, is what remains still viable content?*
2. **There are six kinds of document type — file each in its folder.** Page (renders), Block (renders; lives in block list/grid; never used as a composition), Composition (composed onto others; never rendered, never pickable), Data (element; never renders — settings, events, people), Repository (container node; never renders), Repository Item (the pickable records inside a Repository).
3. **Data types never sit at the root of the data type tree.** Built-ins under `/Umbraco/<editor>`, custom ones under `/Custom/<editor>`. `DataTypeSavedHandler` enforces this on every save.
4. **Register in an `IComposer`, not Program.cs.** If `IUmbracoBuilder` can do it, it belongs in `Composers/`. Non-Umbraco concerns (CORS, App Insights) go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods.
5. **Production runs in production mode.** Umbraco Application Url set, `--configuration Release`, HTTPS only, no model generation, no template editing. `appsettings.json` ships configured this way — don't soften it; put dev conveniences in `appsettings.Development.json`.
6. **Aliases are English and camelCase.** No exceptions.
7. **Dictionary keys are PascalCase with dots** (`My.Dictionary.Item`), and a dictionary folder never has values of its own.
8. **Media always lives in a folder.**
9. **The content root only holds Repositories.** The site hangs under the WWW `siteRoot` node; going multi-site means adding another Page beneath it, not re-architecting. Because WWW never renders, the site Page needs a **domain** or nothing answers on `/` — assign `/` for a single site, a hostname each for several.
10. **uSync everything — commit `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/`.** Export is automatic; you should not need to trigger it. On Umbraco Cloud, use Umbraco Deploy instead.

value.markup:
What is MCP?

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that lets AI models connect securely to the tools, data, and workflows they need — without custom integrations or fragile plumbing.

Think of it as a USB-C port for AI: one protocol, any tool, any provider. Instead of wiring each LLM to each tool individually, MCP gives both sides a common language to negotiate capabilities, exchange context, and execute actions.

Why does it matter?

Before MCP, every AI-tool integration was bespoke. You wrote a custom plugin for OpenAI, another for Anthropic, another for your internal API. Each broke when either side updated. Developers spent more time maintaining connectors than building features.

MCP changes that. It standardises:

  • Resource access — fetching files, database rows, or API responses
  • Tool execution — safely running actions with human oversight
  • Context windows — streaming results back so the model stays grounded

The result? Faster development, fewer bugs, and integrations that work across every major LLM provider.

value.markup:
Getting Started

Building an MCP server is surprisingly straightforward. The protocol is transport-agnostic — you can serve it over stdio (for local tools) or HTTP+SSE (for remote services). The official SDKs for TypeScript, Python, Java, and Kotlin handle the protocol mechanics so you focus on your actual tools.

Your First Tool

An MCP server exposes tools — functions the AI can call with your approval. Each tool has a name, description, and typed parameters. The LLM decides which tool to invoke based on the description, so clear naming is essential.

Here is what a simple weather tool looks like:

@Tool(description: "Get current weather")
fun getWeather(
    @ToolParam(description: "City name") city: String
): String { ... }

Resources and Context

MCP also provides resources — read-only data the AI can pull in. Files, database queries, API responses — anything that helps the model stay accurate. Resources update in real-time, so the AI always works with fresh data.

Together, tools and resources mean the AI can read your database schema, then write a query — all through one protocol. That is the power of MCP.

## ✅ Done — Blog Site Complete

### What was built

A simple blog site about **"Why MCP is Awesome"** powered by Umbraco, created entirely through the Umbraco MCP servers with no manual backoffice clicks.

### Architecture

- **Umbraco v18** with ModelsBuilder (SourceCodeAuto mode)
- **Block Grid** rendering via ViewComponent-per-block pattern (AGENTS.md conventions)
- **Tailwind CSS** via Vite build pipeline
- **10 Unsplash photos** imported into the media library

### Content structure

| Page | URL | Blocks |
|---|---|---|
| Blog Front Page | `/` | Hero + RichText |
| "What is MCP and Why Should You Care?" | `/what-is-mcp-and-why-should-you-care/` | Hero + RichText |
| "Building with MCP: A Practical Guide" | `/building-with-mcp-a-practical-guide/` | Hero + RichText |

### Schema

- **Document types**: `blogFrontPage` (with `blogPost` as allowed child), `blogPost` — both in a Pages folder
- **Element types**: `heroBlock` (heading, text, backgroundImage), `richTextBlock` (content — Tiptap)
- **Data types**: "Blog Block Grid" in a Data folder
- **Templates**: `_Layout`, `BlogFrontPage`, `BlogPost`
- **Domain**: `"/"` assigned to the front page with `en-US`

### Rendering pipeline (AGENTS.md compliant)

- `BlogFrontPage.cshtml` / `BlogPost.cshtml` → `GetBlockGridHtmlAsync(Model, "blocks")`
- `blockgrid/Components/heroBlock.cshtml` → adapter maps `BlockGridItem<HeroBlock>` to `HeroModel` → `Component.InvokeAsync("Hero", ...)`
- `blockgrid/Components/richTextBlock.cshtml` → same pattern for `RichTextModel`
- `Views/Shared/Components/Hero/Default.cshtml` and `RichText/Default.cshtml` → all markup

### How to view

```bash
# Front page
curl -sk https://localhost:44317/

# Blog posts
curl -sk https://localhost:44317/what-is-mcp-and-why-should-you-care/
curl -sk https://localhost:44317/building-with-mcp-a-practical-guide/
```
